description:
NASA Space Apps at UTS: Creating astronaut health software. Led by a Telecommunications Eng Professor providing mentorship in Programming, Networks & Transmission.
Looking for: UI/UX: Clear medical interfaces, Dev/Hardware: Telemetry, IoT, biomedical data.
summary: The Space System for Astronaut Health Monitoring (Espacial para Monitoreo de Salud en Astronautas - SEMSA) is a tool for actively monitoring physical and mental health during space missions. It enables the continuous recording of indicators, data, and personalized information about individuals to identify relevant health trends or risks, thereby generating alerts classified as urgent, preventive, or normal, facilitating the early identification of potential signs of deterioration and supporting decision-making to improve well-being and safety processes within various space environments. SEMSA also serves as a system for recurring notifications aimed at promoting activities related to the group, psychological, and physical well-being of astronauts participating in missions.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

SEMSA is a software platform designed to support the comprehensive monitoring of astronauts' health and well-being during space missions. Its purpose is to centralize information related to the physical, psychological, and cognitive conditions of crew members, facilitating access to relevant indicators, monitoring their progress, and identifying potential situations that may require attention. 

Through the organization and visualization of this data, the platform aims to provide structured information that facilitates health monitoring and supports decision-making processes by astronauts and mission teams. 

What benefits does it have?

SEMSA provides an organized and interactive visualization of astronauts' health status through a summary of physiological indicators and the ability to explore specific variables, as well as their historical records and trends. The platform addresses different dimensions of health related to the skeletal, neurological, cardiovascular, metabolic, integumentary, muscular, and locomotor systems. 

To facilitate interaction with this information, the platform proposes the use of an interactive anatomical model that allows users to explore variables associated with different body regions or systems. Additionally, the platform incorporates mechanisms for classifying and displaying alerts to highlight indicators that may require monitoring or further review. 

Another feature of SEMSA is the incorporation of preventive and wellness activities aimed at encouraging healthy habits and promoting the monitoring of physical, psychological, and cognitive conditions throughout the mission. These activities may focus on collecting physiological information, assessing emotional well-being, monitoring cognitive abilities, reviewing environmental conditions, strengthening health education, and maintaining communication with the mission team.

What is the intended impact of the project?

SEMSA aims to contribute to astronauts' health, safety, and well-being during long-duration space missions through an integrated and personalized monitoring approach. The platform is intended to facilitate the early identification of potential risk situations and provide information that supports the adoption of preventive measures. 

Furthermore, it addresses aspects related to physical, psychological, and cognitive well-being, as well as the effects of isolation and confinement. To this end, it promotes the inclusion of recreational activities, healthy habits, and mechanisms that encourage social connection during missions. 

Overall, SEMSA seeks to support informed decision-making by astronauts and mission teams, contributing to the development of strategies for safer and more sustainable space exploration. 

 What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your Project?

We built SEMSA as a full-stack web application.

Backend: We wrote the backend in Python. We used FastAPI with Uvicorn for the REST API, SQLAlchemy for the database layer, Pydantic to validate data, httpx for HTTP requests and pytest for automated testing. The database schema is written in SQL and works with both SQLite and PostgreSQL. The forecasting engine is our own statistical model in Python. It uses robust trend estimation, linear regression (OLS) and calibrated prediction intervals, and it does not depend on external machine-learning libraries.

Frontend: The interface uses HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript with native ES modules, without a framework. We drew all the charts ourselves in SVG, without charting libraries. The interactive 3D Solar System runs on native WebGL with GLSL shaders, adapted from the open-source repo-planets project. The fonts are IBM Plex from Google Fonts.

Infrastructure and tools: We packaged the app with Docker and Docker Compose and deployed it to a Linux VPS, which we also used to run tests in disposable containers. We managed the code with Git and GitHub and used Claude Code as an AI coding assistant.

How is your Project creative?

SEMSA incorporates several elements designed to facilitate the monitoring of astronauts’ health and well-being:

Interactivity: The platform presents physiological indicators in a summarized format through an interactive anatomical model. This feature allows users to review the status of variables using priority classifications (low, medium, and high) and access historical information to observe their evolution. Furthermore, the proposed approach considers a comprehensive perspective on well-being that extends beyond biomedical measurements.

Data visualization: SEMSA includes its own interactive charts, built from scratch without external libraries:

Indicator trends: Each health indicator shows a mini trend line next to its current value. When users select an indicator, a detailed chart shows its full history over the mission. Yellow and red bands mark the caution and critical limits, and a line shows the astronaut’s personal baseline, so deviations are easy to spot at a glance. The charts have tooltips and can be explored with the mouse, by touch or with the keyboard, and screen readers announce each value.

Physiological forecasting: Astronauts can see where their own indicators are heading in the coming days. The forecast chart shows 80% and 95% prediction bands, warns early if a value is likely to cross a clinical threshold, and offers a preventive recommendation. The model only shows a trend when it proves reliable on the astronaut’s own data, and it was calibrated with real NASA bed-rest data, a ground analog of microgravity. It is exploratory and never a diagnosis.

One chart per analysis engine: The mission logbook gathers a chart for each engine: forecasts, alerts per day, cognitive performance by domain, emotional check-ins, sleep and early signs of isolation, and accumulated radiation dose against its limit. If an engine has no data to show, SEMSA explains why instead of drawing an empty chart.

Radiation monitoring: A real-time chart shows the radiation dose rate on a logarithmic scale, with an orange line marking the threshold at which the crew must take shelter. It replays real data from the HERA sensors aboard Orion during the Artemis I mission and can simulate a solar particle event, so the crew can practice the shelter procedure.

Cognitive progress: The cognitive module shows how accuracy changes over time in each cognitive domain. It does not reduce performance to a single score.

Visual radiation alerts: When radiation reaches a medium or high level, the whole radiation module flashes every five seconds in yellow (caution), orange (warning) or red (emergency). The alert bar at the top of the screen also blinks until a crew member acknowledges the alert. This way, a critical event is noticed even when the user is focused on another task. For users sensitive to motion, the flashing is turned off and the alert stays visible without animation.

Dynamic environments and interactive 3D Solar System: SEMSA adapts its health information to five mission environments: spacecraft, space station, rover, planetary base on Mars and lunar surface. For the selected environment, an interactive chart compares its key hazards, the priority of each body system together with the astronaut’s current status, and its typical radiation and exercise needs against the other environments. Next to it, an interactive 3D model of the Solar System, rendered in real time with WebGL, smoothly moves the camera to the selected environment and follows it along its orbit. This turns an abstract setting into something the crew can see and explore.

Preventive and wellness activities: The incorporation of recurring activities related to different dimensions of health aims to complement indicator monitoring with actions intended to encourage healthy habits, reinforce self-care, and address potential physical, psychological, and cognitive needs.

Gamification: The project incorporates an experience points (XP) and progression-level system designed to encourage astronauts’ participation in and continued engagement with the proposed activities. This mechanism recognizes consistency and learning without penalizing users based on their physiological measurement results.

Psychological and social well-being: SEMSA incorporates recreational activities, opportunities for personal expression, self-care, social interaction with crew members, and guidance on keeping in touch with loved ones on Earth. These elements aim to promote emotional well-being and help mitigate some of the effects associated with isolation and confinement during space missions.

What factors did your team consider? 

The team considered several factors related to astronauts' conditions and needs during space missions, including physical and psychological health, emotional well-being, social connection, cognitive performance, and the potential effects of isolation and confinement. 

The team also considered environmental conditions specific to the space environment, the challenges associated with long-duration missions, the individual needs of crew members, and the importance of preventive health monitoring. NASA research and findings related to human health in space were considered as references for the proposed solution, along with the importance of safety protocols and personalized health monitoring.
